Meeting header:
Date: 2028-06-07
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth CTO), Lina Torres (VelaHealth DevOps), Evan Park (VelaHealth PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Discussed recent uptime blips and burn rate on committed Dedicated pool.
- Reviewed tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private VPC given regulatory constraints.
- Agreed on next steps: Redwood to send SLA commitment numbers and SE docs; VelaHealth to run a targeted synthetic test and share traces.

Topics: uptime incidents, SLA/burn rate, cost optimization, private deployment timeline, KV cache behavior, SOC2/audit logs, roadmap prioritization.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex Kim (Redwood): ok everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, this is Alex from Redwood, with Priya our SE, uh quick check on time we have about an hour, is that still good?
[00:14] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): yep that's perfect, thanks. we've got a couple of ops folks listening in too.
[00:20] Priya Nair (Redwood): hi all, I'll jump into the technicals after Alex covers the SLA questions and the burn-rate overview.
[00:29] Evan Park (VelaHealth): quick note, we saw two 5-10m degradations last week during our batch inference window, want to understand why and the mitigation options.
[00:36] Alex Kim (Redwood): got it. so first, quick status: since the last check-in you scaled the dedicated pool from 8->12 cards, right? Lina?
[00:44] Lina Torres (VelaHealth): correct. we activated burst capacity for two days to cover peak, which bumped spend... the burn rate on committed credits spiked. we also saw a small number of timeouts, some 503-ish responses.
[00:56] Priya Nair (Redwood): okay that matches what our telemetry shows. there were two short periods where autoscaler lagged behind surge; I want to caveat though, the logs are a bit noisy and the autoscaler is set to conservative thresholds.
[01:12] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): can you explain the autoscaler behavior? and why it didn't pick up faster?
[01:18] Priya Nair (Redwood): sure — our Dedicated autoscaler is a mix of queue-length and GPU-util signals, and if there's a sudden burst from long-seq requests it can take, like, 30-90s to spin up additional instances depending on the policy. additionally if KV cache cold-starts are happening, those token latencies compound.
[01:36] Evan Park (VelaHealth): so is the hot path here the long sequence/prefix traffic? we do a lot of multi-step chart summarizations that have big context.
[01:43] Priya Nair (Redwood): yes, long-context is the culprit. also quantization variant selection matters — you were on the 4-bit quantized variant which is great for throughput but can increase decode time for long-seq? (slight laugh) it's a weird tradeoff.
[01:57] Alex Kim (Redwood): on the SLA side — the committed pool SLA covers 99.5% availability for inference endpoints and we publish p50/p90 latencies per model family. but we also need to look at your success criteria — you mentioned you need 99.9 for core endpoints during business hours?
[02:12] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): yes for our triage routing and clinical alerts we need much higher availability during business hours. 99.5 just yields too much risk for us.
[02:21] Alex Kim (Redwood): understood. two levers we discussed before: dedicated sizing + prewarmed capacity (reserve warm instances) and prefix/KV cache warming for frequent sessions. Priya, can you explain the prewarm idea?
[02:33] Priya Nair (Redwood): prewarm keeps standby replicas with KV cache warmed for your common prefixes; that reduces the first-token latency dramatically. it costs, obviously, because those GPUs are reserved and billed. another option is burst with faster spin-up by using smaller, prebuilt image pools that have lower boot time.
[02:51] Lina Torres (VelaHealth): what's the estimated cost delta between prewarm and burst? the burn rate last month was painful.
[02:58] Alex Kim (Redwood): rough numbers: prewarm equals about 15-25% higher baseline spend depending on how many warm replicas. burst is cheaper on baseline but increases the chance of a short outage if autoscaler is slow. we'll run a short cost model and show p50 cost per thousand tokens.
[03:14] Evan Park (VelaHealth): can you also show cost normalized by successful inference vs error retries? retries are sneaky.
[03:20] Priya Nair (Redwood): yep we'll include retry overhead. also we recommend prefix caching if you have predictable conversation starts — that reduces repeated token compute.
[03:30] [00:03:30] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): on compliance, we need to confirm audit logs, KMS integration, and namespaced RBAC — if we go private VPC we need to ensure our audit pipeline receives the same event detail.
[03:43] Alex Kim (Redwood): absolutely — for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and forward audit logs via our log-forwarder; we support SAML/SSO for console and token scoping. note though some field names in the logs are internal and our docs sometimes call them different things, apologies for that inconsistency — we'll send the mapping.
[03:58] Priya Nair (Redwood): and also, for SOC2 related artifacts, we have the compliance pack and a compliance liaison who can jump on a separate call if you want to run a quick audit checklist.
[04:08] Lina Torres (VelaHealth): yes please. we need to align our security reviewers before the procurement window.
[04:12] Alex Kim (Redwood): makes sense. procurement timeline — where are you in buying cycle? Evan?
[04:17] Evan Park (VelaHealth): aiming for a pilot in July and decision by August, but that's soft. executives want hard numbers for run-rate and a mitigation plan if latency breaches happen.
[04:27] Alex Kim (Redwood): ok pilot July — we can scope a 4-week POC: two core endpoints behind dedicated pool, synthetic traffic, and the private VPC checklist. Priya will scope the test plan.

[04:40] Priya Nair (Redwood): on the technical plan: we'll do a baseline load with current config, then run a cold-start simulation, and finally test prewarm vs burst. for traces, please attach application request IDs and the redwood request id (we'll share header name). the more we have, the faster root cause.
[04:58] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): request IDs, got it. also can you explain the KV cache TTL behavior? sometimes we see stale values in returned contexts.
[05:06] Priya Nair (Redwood): sure — KV cache is per-replica and we have an LRU eviction policy; if you run multiple replicas without sticky session you may hit misses when the request hits a different replica. enabling session-affinity for clinical flows helps. also TTLs are settable per-route but default to 600s.
[05:24] Evan Park (VelaHealth): session-affinity would help, but that also impacts load distribution. is there an automatic affinity that respects evenness?
[05:31] Priya Nair (Redwood): we have a hashing-based affinity that tries to keep even distribution, but high-cardinality sessions can still create hot shards. we'll show sharding patterns from your workload.
[05:44] [00:05:44] Lina Torres (VelaHealth): how about model variants — you mentioned quant and non-quant variants. can we fallback to a slower higher-precision model during peaks?
[05:52] Alex Kim (Redwood): yes, that's a routing policy we often use — route to quant variant by default, fallback to fp16 on errors or high-latency. the tradeoff is cost; fp16 can be 30-60% more expensive per token.
[06:04] Priya Nair (Redwood): and we can do gradual rollouts with canary percentages to measure quality delta. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization settings per workload — we'll include recommended profiles.
[06:18] Evan Park (VelaHealth): are there any quick wins to reduce spend without hurting availability?
[06:23] Alex Kim (Redwood): yes — intelligent batching, response truncation for non-critical endpoints, and adaptive quant selection. also TTL tuning for short-lived caches. small config changes often yield 10-25% savings.
[06:35] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): ok, let's talk concrete numbers — what will you send us after this call?
[06:40] Alex Kim (Redwood): we'll send: 1) an SLA/latency playbook with committed numbers and prewarm pricing, 2) a POC test plan and scripts for synthetic load, 3) a KV cache + session-affinity best-practice doc, 4) a short compliance artifact map for SOC2/KMS/logs.
[06:55] Evan Park (VelaHealth): good. if we do POC, can Redwood spin up a temporary dedicated pool in our target region?
[07:02] Priya Nair (Redwood): yes, we can allocate a short-lived dedicated pool for POC, region permitting. note provisioning lead time is usually 24-48h if capacity is available.
[07:12] Lina Torres (VelaHealth): last question — do you provide automated guardrails to downgrade quality gracefully if capacity is exhausted? we want to avoid full outage.
[07:20] Alex Kim (Redwood): yes — we support graceful degradation rules: automatic fallback to cheaper model, token limit enforcement, and rate-based shedding with informative response codes. You can configure per-route policies in the console or via API.
[07:36] [00:07:36] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): perfect. any risks we should be aware of?
[07:41] Priya Nair (Redwood): main risk is cold-KV starts for long-context workloads, and autoscaler tuning; both are manageable with prewarm and affinity. we'll show the failure cases in the POC.
[07:53] Alex Kim (Redwood): ok let's capture next steps — we're aligned on the POC and SLA docs. anything else from Vela?
[07:59] Evan Park (VelaHealth): just to ensure we get raw traces and cost model.
[08:03] Lina Torres (VelaHealth): and compliance liaison contact.
[08:07] Alex Kim (Redwood): got it. Priya will send the SE docs, I'll send SLA playbook and pricing.
[08:12] Priya Nair (Redwood): I'll share the KV cache and warm-up checklist and a starter script for synthetic traffic.
[08:18] [00:08:18] (crosstalk, brief)
[08:24] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): one more — we sometimes see the console usage spikes causing quota-based throttles on keys, do you have suggested key-level rate limits to avoid that?
[08:34] Alex Kim (Redwood): yes, set per-key quotas for your non-critical clients and reserve high-priority tokens for production. we also recommend app-layer backoff to prevent thundering herd.
[08:46] Evan Park (VelaHealth): will you send an example quota profile?
[08:50] Priya Nair (Redwood): yes, example files included.
[08:54] Alex Kim (Redwood): ok final recap: Redwood delivers SLA docs by 2028-06-10; Vela runs 48h synthetic test and returns traces by 2028-06-20; schedule the pilot provisioning week of 2028-06-24; compliance liaison call to follow.
[09:09] Dr. Marcus Chen (VelaHealth): thanks all, this was productive.
[09:14] Alex Kim (Redwood): thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with attachments. bye.
